newsitem.title: Austria: Bank Austria gets Creditanstalt in overnight deal. [CORRECTED 23:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Bank Austria gets Creditanstalt in overnight deal. [CORRECTED 23:30 GMT]

text.p: Austrians woke up on Sunday to news that august bank Creditanstalt had finally been sold to arch-rival Bank Austria, ending after seven years longest running privatisation drama.

After an 11-hour crisis meeting of coalition leaders that dragged into the early hours of Sunday, the feuding partners hammered out a deal that let both sides save face -- but which will shake up the Alpine republic's bloated banking sector.

"I can tell you that the state's stake in Creditanstalt will go to the highest bidder which is Bank Austria," Chancellor Franz Vranitzky said, closing the chapter on a sale which deeply divided the coalition and threatened the survival of the government.

Creditanstalt, established in 1855 to finance the development of Europe's railway network under Austro-Hungarian imperial rule, is to retain its independence for the next five years. Over the next seven years (corrects from five years), Bank Austria will gradually be taken out of public control.
Full privatisation of Austria's top bank, controlled by the City of Vienna and part state-owned, was a key demand of the conservatives and a stumbling block in the negotiations.
Another conservative demand was to ensure Creditanstalt's small shareholders received a competitive price.

Social Democrat Finance Minister Viktor Klima, in charge of the privatisation, said Bank Austria would offer small shareholders an extra two schillings per ordinary share to buy the 30 percent of voting shares not yet owned by the state -- a premium of 0.3 percent over their market price.
Bank Austria would also distribute shares worth a total 500 million schillings to the small shareholders, which Klima said Bank Austria would finance out of its own capital resources.

According to the coalition agreement, the state's 19 percent stake in Bank Austria will be floated immediately, while the 45 percent stake held by the City of Vienna's Anteilsverwaltung Zentralsparkasse (AVZ) foundation is to be cut to below 20 percent within seven years.

AVZ guarantees Bank Austria's liabilities, ensuring it a AAA rating, but the conservatives want AVZ's financial responsibility removed fully, which would be likely to cost Bank Austria its top rating and an extra 100 million schillings per year to finance its debt.
The reduction of AVZ's stake would be achieved through a series of capital increases in which the foundation would not take part, Klima said.

People's Party leader Wolfgang Schuessel, who lost his battle to keep Creditanstalt firmly in the conservative camp but scored on a number of side issues, said it had not been easy for his party to agree to Bank Austria as the winner.
"This was a very hard but also a very good round of talks. The decision wasn't easy for us," he said after the meeting.

The two banks will have combined assets of about 14 billion schillings ($1.26 billion) and control a major part of Austria's retail and wholesale banking market. Together, they hold wide-reaching interests in the country's key industries.
Bank Austria is expected to outline its strategy for Creditanstalt at a news conference at 1 p.m. (1200 GMT), while Klima is scheduled to release further details of the deal at 11 a.m. (1000 GMT).
The international consortium of industrial and financial interests led by insurer EA-Generali, who lost out in the race, said it regretted the finance minister's decision.
"We submitted....the most attractive offer for the long-term good of Austria's economy," the group's spokesman and EA-Generali chief executive Dietrich Karner said in a brief statement.
The consortium was outbid by some two billion schillings.
